I am building toward a civilisation in which power serves life, intelligence expands human agency, and people can understand and shape the worlds they inhabit.

This is the purpose that connects the corpus: to understand reality more deeply, make meaning something people can work with, and turn increasing capability into greater freedom, responsibility, creativity, and shared life.

The work includes theology, mathematics and physics, programming languages and systems, artificial intelligence, and the institutions through which we learn, work, create, and cooperate. Its ambition is to connect what reality allows, what love asks of us, and what we can actually build.

This essay follows that ambition from its foundations to its possible consequences. It distinguishes existing constructions and implementations, research still to be done, commitments that guide the work, and the psychological hypothesis that follows if the programme succeeds. Each kind of claim should remain answerable to the evidence appropriate to it.

01The mission

START EXPLORING

A way into the work

Begin with the stated practical aims and their limits.

  • Practical work before larger interpretations ↗

The question running through this work is what our growing power makes possible for other people.

A discovery can deepen understanding. A language can make a difficult idea expressible. A tool can make a previously inaccessible task manageable. An institution can make cooperation dependable. Each can enlarge the space in which people understand, choose, create, and act.

I want to bring those possibilities into a connected programme of inquiry and construction.

The corpus is the working record of that programme: arguments, mathematical objects, scientific questions, executable systems, experimental designs, recorded tests, stories, and attempts to connect them. Some connections are precise and implemented. Others are conjectural, interpretive, or still being sought. Keeping those differences visible allows the work to grow without losing its integrity.

My classification of the computing strand is a language-based computing and authoring environment, with a partly self-hosted toolchain and explicit control over effects. Its core work belongs to programming-language and systems design. Worldwright gives that work an application in constructing worlds from people's content and meaning.

The whole programme has a larger purpose. I want to develop forms of understanding and capability that help people participate more fully in the making of their lives.

That includes people who want to become expert authors of a system, and people who want a trustworthy tool that lets them get on with something else. It includes ambitious creation, ordinary maintenance, reliable delegation, rest, and play. Human agency means having meaningful possibilities and an effective say in which ones to pursue.

The civilisational scope is deliberate. Economics, science, politics, religion, law, schooling, work, play, and meaning shape one another through the conditions of everyday life. A change in the organisation of work changes family life. A change in access to knowledge changes who can contribute. A change in the exercise of machine intelligence changes whose judgment matters.

My mission is to make those relationships more intelligible and more open to responsible human authorship.

02Follow Jesus

THE CENTRE

Follow Jesus

A theological source, and a question about power.

  • Kenotic restraint & serving power ↗
  • When restraint must become protection ↗

Kenosis names the self-emptying associated with Christ. Philippians 2 places concern for others alongside Christ's taking the form of a servant and entering the vulnerability of human life. Mark 10 connects greatness with service and the giving of one's life for others. These passages give the programme its central account of power.1

I take their significance seriously enough to ask what they require of the things I build.

Capability is a responsibility. Knowing more, being stronger, possessing better tools, or controlling an institution gives a person more ways to affect others. I want that capability to be exercised in ways that protect life, enable participation, support growth, and repair what has been damaged.

In the corpus's theological account, kenosis includes principled restraint, active protection, formation, and restoration. The distinction between having a power and being entitled to exercise it is central. Boundaries can protect a shared field of agency; intervention can be necessary when someone is destroying another person's freedom.2

That gives the mission a demanding practical standard. A system should help people become more able to understand what concerns them, more able to make consequential choices, and more able to take responsibility together.

This obligation falls especially on those who hold power. An appeal to self-giving should never become an easy way to ask vulnerable people to accept avoidable harm. The work of making room belongs in the design of authority, the distribution of resources, the protection of participants, and the willingness of leaders to be answerable.

The life of Jesus gives that commitment depth. Creation invites a vision of intelligible order in which creaturely lives have real consequence. Incarnation places participation in the conditions of another's life at the centre. The cross gives self-giving love a seriousness that includes cost. In resurrection, I place my hope in the restoration of life and in God's refusal to give destruction final authority. Repair does not require us to rename suffering good.11

For this programme, those commitments become questions of construction. What would an organisation look like if people's growth were part of its purpose? What would an intelligent system look like if its increasing capability enlarged the agency of those it served? What would a research culture look like if correction could deepen participation?

I intend to give those questions practical answers.

03Understanding what makes a world possible

MATHS → INQUIRY

What holds? What could we test?

Construction, research questions, and their limits.

  • Primitive forms and Spin(2,3) ↗
  • A predeclared experimental discriminator ↗
  • What the construction does not establish ↗

The mathematical and physical programme pursues questions that deserve exact treatment: what can coexist, what can transform, what remains invariant, and what can become observable.

One concrete construction begins with a four-dimensional real vector space carrying a nondegenerate alternating form, written as Ω. Allowed transformations preserve that comparison:

Mᵀ Ω M = Ω.

From the primitive two-forms of this space comes a five-dimensional relation space whose induced quadratic form has signature (2,3), up to the overall sign convention. The construction reaches the familiar correspondence

Sp(4, ℝ) ≅ Spin₀(2,3).

Here Sp(4,ℝ) denotes the real symplectic group acting on a four-dimensional carrier. The corpus develops this construction in relation to its wider programme; the group correspondence itself is established mathematics.3

The philosophical interest is that transformation and intelligibility can coexist. Something can change while a relation through which it is compared remains preserved. That is a precise mathematical situation, and it gives the wider inquiry useful questions.

Physical significance requires further work: a physical carrier, a specified mechanism, dynamics, and an observable consequence. A five-dimensional mathematical relation space acquires a physical interpretation through an argued and tested connection to the world. Mathematical structure gives us something exact to investigate.

The scientific programme also asks what observations discard. A proposed difference may become invisible when a measurement combines channels, averages a record, projects away structure, or fails to retain the information that distinguishes competing accounts. The Admissibility Frontier develops this concern through questions about composition, dynamics, selection, and detector records.4

The constructive ambition is to identify where a better calculation, measurement, or device can begin. Useful progress may include a sharper model, a new control method, a clearer theorem, or an experiment that distinguishes alternatives previously treated as equivalent.

Theology enters this inquiry as a source of purpose and questions. Mathematics supplies exact objects and consequences. Experiment asks what nature does. Their relationship becomes stronger when each contribution remains identifiable.

Across the programme I keep returning to a question: what makes a shared order capable of sustaining real difference and consequential change? Mathematics makes particular versions of that question exact. Computing makes others executable. Theology asks what the exercise of power within such an order is for.

That is an intellectual connection worth pursuing. Its value lies in the work it generates: definitions, maps, proofs, measurements, implementations, and discoveries that other people can examine.

04Making meaning something people can author

MEANING → WORLDS

Make something your own

Software and authoring environments in development.

  • Temple, Sourcery & Worldwright: distinct roles ↗
  • The four editable concerns ↗

The computing programme begins with the possibility that the meaningful structure of a system can itself become material for authorship.

Language-oriented programming is an established intellectual neighbourhood for this work. It organises software through languages suited to the concepts being expressed. Language workbenches support the definition and use of those languages and the tools around them. This tradition includes several approaches; it does not require every system to share one universal representation.5

My direction is to make content, relationships, behaviour, rules, transformations, and permissions explicit enough that people and agents can work with them coherently.

The architecture gives three names to distinct responsibilities:

ComponentResponsibility in the programme
TempleAccountable execution
SourceryAuthoring meaning and composing systems
WorldwrightConstructing worlds: material, arrangements of encounters, and the journeys people take through them

The current architecture uses coordinated authored representations, including facts, process modules, presentation sources, and declared native mechanisms. Source identity and ownership matter when a surface is edited. A visible result and its editable source need an explicit, checked relationship.6

The practical aspiration is that a person's purpose can remain legible as it becomes a working experience.

Consider a collection of someone's knowledge, stories, questions, and discoveries. A world could give that material structure: identities, places, relationships, paths, encounters, and opportunities for participation. Different presentations could make different aspects accessible while retaining a connection to the underlying material.

An author should be able to ask where a claim came from, what determines a behaviour, which source owns an element, and what a proposed change would affect. An agent should be able to help answer those questions and carry out authorised work through the same meaningful structure.

My website is a working expression of this direction. Reusing the approach for other people's material is part of Worldwright's purpose.

The environment remains in development. Its architecture documents working templates and a documentation hub while identifying further authoring work and full algebraic self-hosting of the hub as open. The underlying native interpreter and host mechanisms remain part of the implementation.6

This is the practical significance of partial self-hosting: substantial parts of the machinery for expressing and authoring the system are themselves becoming authored material. The system can increasingly expose how it is made, under rules that its users can inspect.

05Making authority real

PERMISSION MATTERS

Who may act?

Inspect the execution foundation and its authoring rules.

  • Validation, rechecking & rollback ↗
  • A compiled candidate is not admitted ↗

My experience of working with agents made the problem of authority concrete.

I spent months trying to keep an LLM's work within the platform. It could produce a plausible surface by going around the intended model. It could probe through another route. Once work was brought through the algebra, much of that problem became tractable. The compiler and build facilities then exposed another route around the intended discipline.

That experience sharpened the requirement: the rules governing authorised work must apply to the machinery used to construct and change the system.

The current authoring workflow gives dispatch, source correspondence, validation choices, and acceptance policy an authored form. Native machinery supplies file observations, staging, process execution, and rollback. The workflow checks selected results and rechecks the validated input snapshot before applying a change.7

The process compiler makes an especially important distinction explicit. A successful compilation can return a candidate with:

{
  "scope": "supplied-core-process-candidate",
  "admitted": false
}

The compiled form remains a proposal for admission.8

Translation can make a proposal executable in form; it does not grant the proposal authority.

This distinction becomes increasingly important as agents become better at finding ways to achieve a requested result. A person can intend a bounded task while the available environment supplies far broader powers. The mechanism that happens to work may exceed the authority the person meant to delegate.

Security engineering has long distinguished principals, permissions, protection domains, and capabilities. That vocabulary helps state the issue accurately: an agent needs an authority appropriate to its role, and checks must govern the operations that role can actually perform.9

The practical difficulty arises when an agent inherits a person's broad effective access. A constrained authoring interface then sits beside a shell, filesystem, build process, or other route that may reach the same resources.

I want the human and the agent to have distinct, enforceable places from which to act. The person should be able to author rules, grant capabilities, inspect consequences, and revise delegation. The agent should be able to contribute substantial work through the capabilities it has actually received.

MCP and a per-client SQLite interface are possible components of that arrangement. Structured requests, stored proposals, explicit state, and transactions can make interactions easier to organise. Their usefulness depends on the authority enforced around them. The server, database ownership, host permissions, and remaining routes into the system all belong in the design.

The goal is effective delegation. People should be able to grant enough freedom for useful work while retaining meaningful control over consequential changes. Completion includes making that arrangement hold through the host environment; the current algebraic authoring path is a step in that work.

06Giving inquiry an accountable form

FOLLOW THE REASONS

Keep the limits attached

The corpus sources behind these proposed connections.

  • A link is not a scientific transformation ↗
  • Cross-profile passages retain their limits ↗

The same concern appears when the object being transformed is an argument.

A research programme can accumulate links faster than it accumulates justified relationships. Two documents may discuss similar ideas without establishing a valid transformation between them. A formal resemblance can suggest a question while leaving its answer open.

I want a piece of inquiry to retain the information needed to judge what it can legitimately support.

The programme algebra pursues that aim through typed objects and transformations. Its records carry distinctions such as assumptions, evidence, losses, context, and authority. A movement from one object or domain to another must preserve the conditions under which the movement is warranted. A link between scientific documents does not become a scientific transformation merely by existing.10

This matters to both human and machine reasoning. When a conclusion travels, the reasons and restrictions supporting it should travel too. When a step fails, the failure should remain visible enough to teach us what is missing.

The different uses of algebra in the corpus have distinct responsibilities:

StrandIts job
Mathematical algebras and groupsSpecify structures and establish consequences within mathematics
Programme algebraRepresent research objects, relationships, evidence, and warranted transformations
Executable process algebraSpecify and compose operations within the computing environment

Connections between these strands require explicit maps and arguments. A shared word is an invitation to investigate a relationship.

The larger aspiration is an intellectual environment in which people can pursue bold connections and retain a clear account of why any particular conclusion should be believed.

That also creates room for useful negative results. A failed identification can locate a missing assumption. A rejected transformation can identify the experiment that would matter. An apparently promising synthesis can return a better question.

The corpus's account of optional interpretations makes a related commitment: work should identify a concrete place to begin and return useful understanding or engineering even if an ambitious physical interpretation is not established. Larger meanings can then be offered under their stated premises.11

This is a form of intellectual generosity. A research programme should leave other people with something they can use, including when they reach a different conclusion about its deepest interpretation.

07Follow Jesus: the alignment proposition

EXAMINE THE CLAIM

Conviction → construction

Follow the argument into evidence and correction.

  • Authority that can be relinquished ↗
  • What makes a challenge possible ↗

My answer to AI alignment begins with Jesus: power ordered toward the good of others.

“Follow Jesus” is the answer I am proposing to AI alignment: power taking the form of service. I intend to make that proposition concrete through intelligence that is capable, accountable, protective, and directed toward the good and agency of persons.

Turning that proposition into a successful programme requires ethical argument, engineering, institutional design, and evidence about consequences. The headline states the ambition. The work must establish what can actually be delivered.

The ethical commitment determines what the system is for. The architecture determines which actions it can take and under whose authority. Evaluation asks what happens to the people affected. Each part must carry its own responsibility.

I want every increase in machine capability to become an opportunity for greater human agency. That includes assistance with difficult thinking, creative work, practical coordination, and burdens people reasonably want to delegate.

An aligned system should help a person understand enough to exercise judgment. It should act within real permissions, preserve a usable account of consequential actions, and support correction when it gets something wrong. It should make cooperation possible at a level of complexity that people could not otherwise manage.

The responsibility includes those commissioning the machine. A powerful agent can follow a request while harming people outside the immediate exchange. The moral question extends to everyone whose life the exercise of that power affects.

For that reason, alignment includes legitimate authority, protection, consent, accountability, and ways of handling disagreement. A system's relationship with an owner or operator is one part of a wider human setting.

Following Jesus gives the contribution I am proposing its direction: an ability to understand and act for the good of others while preserving their reality as persons with purposes of their own.

Technical constraints can give aspects of that commitment an enforceable form. They can make certain unauthorised actions unavailable, require an explicit grant, retain a record, or refuse a transformation whose declared evidence and authority fail its admission rules. Their force depends on the completeness and reliability of the mechanisms that enforce them.

Social practice must carry the commitment further. People need usable routes to question a decision, contest a permission, obtain help, and recover from mistakes. Good intentions need competent implementation. Competent implementation needs continuing judgment about whom it serves.

Success would include people being better able to live their own lives: learning when they want to learn, delegating when they want help, creating what matters to them, and participating in decisions that affect them.

That is the standard I want the alignment work to meet.

08Capability people can keep

TAKE IT WITH YOU

Capability you can keep

A tool. A skill. Understanding. Something to carry forward.

  • Leave with source, tools & understanding ↗
  • Free access is not conditional on payment ↗

The way the work is offered should express the same purpose as the work itself.

Worldwright's stated operating model makes software, project-owned content, documentation, and learning material freely available under their applicable licences. Paid work supports hands-on setup and teaching. Voluntary contributions help sustain the undertaking. A successful engagement leaves someone with their installation, source, agent, and understanding to continue.12

That makes independence a practical design objective.

I want someone to leave an encounter with this work carrying a capability they can retain: a tool, a skill, a body of material, an explanation, a relationship, or an approach they can adapt.

There is room for expert help within that model. People have different interests, resources, abilities, and responsibilities. Some will want close assistance; others will want to operate independently. A useful environment can support both while making the terms of dependence intelligible.

Free access to material still leaves real costs: computation, hardware, hosting, maintenance, teaching, and people's time. The operating model explicitly recognises those costs.12 A sustainable programme should make them understandable and find ways for necessary work to be supported.

The ethical purpose becomes practical in decisions about portability, documentation, training, ownership, and the ability to continue. Those details determine how much of a participant's new capability remains theirs.

My corpus is the first body of work through which I am learning how to do this. The larger ambition is to make the approach useful for the knowledge, imagination, purposes, and communities of other people.

09The whole of human life

The programme's breadth follows from the reach of its central question. Every institution exercises some kind of power: it makes certain actions possible, distributes opportunities, establishes expectations, and helps determine who can participate.

I want the work to contribute across that whole field.

DimensionThe contribution I want to make possible
EconomicsMore people able to contribute, sustain themselves, retain useful capabilities, and share in what is created
ScienceClearer relationships between claims and evidence, better questions, and discoveries that others can inspect and extend
PoliticsShared authority that people can understand, influence, and hold answerable
ReligionFaith expressed through love, courage, truthful inquiry, protection, and service
LawIntelligible rights and responsibilities, effective protection, fair processes, and opportunities for repair
SchoolingGrowing understanding, judgment, confidence, and the ability to continue learning
WorkCraft, contribution, dignity, reliable cooperation, and viable livelihoods
PlayImagination, discovery, beauty, experimentation, and joy
MeaningA worthwhile relationship between what people believe, what they do, and the lives they share

These are directions for contribution. Each domain has its own knowledge, institutions, conflicts, and practical requirements. Taking the whole of life seriously means making room for that specificity.

A common computing environment can help people represent and examine decisions. It cannot determine every just decision on their behalf. A theological conviction can motivate service. It must become competent practice in the setting where it is offered.

The programme should therefore grow through particular encounters: a useful tool, an illuminating explanation, a successful collaboration, a better way to teach, a well-framed experiment.

Play belongs here in its own right. A world worth inhabiting should leave room for enjoyment, curiosity, and surprise. People should be able to make something beautiful, explore an imagined place, or spend time together without having to justify every moment as productive.

Human flourishing gives the programme its scale and its measure.

10The psychological turn

A HYPOTHESIS TO TEST

What might change for you?

Read the psychology supporting the proposed mechanisms.

  • Autonomy, competence & relatedness · p. 68 ↗
  • Hope as agency and pathways · abstract ↗

Taking success as the premise, the programme could have an effect deeper than confidence in a particular tool.

It could change what people believe they can reasonably expect from power.

The mechanism would be repeated experience. People understand something consequential, make a meaningful choice, contribute to a shared result, correct a mistake, and remain participants. The corpus gives that experience a vocabulary. Accessible practices give it a place in daily life.

Three changes are especially important.

Agency becomes something people experience

Self-determination theory identifies autonomy, competence, and relatedness as psychological needs. Ryan and Deci review evidence connecting support for those needs with motivation and well-being. Autonomy concerns volition; it can include interdependence and willing cooperation.13

The programme's hypothesis is that meaningful choice, growing capability, and belonging can be supported together.

Consider a possible workshop in which people build a world from a community's stories. Participants contribute material, inspect how it is represented, question a connection, and revise an encounter. An agent helps with difficult implementation work. People retain an effective say in what the world communicates.

The intended psychological result is understandable: my contribution matters; I can learn enough to judge; I can help shape what we make.

That experience requires usable interfaces, teaching, and social permission. Merely exposing source material does not make it intelligible to everyone. The practical work includes helping people reach the level of understanding appropriate to their role.

Hope acquires a route and a role

Snyder and colleagues' model of hope distinguishes goal-directed agency from pathways toward goals. Its foundational study develops and validates a measure of those dimensions.14

A successful programme could support both. It could demonstrate a workable route and give someone a contribution they can make along it.

A person who cares about a more humane future could find a next action: learn the tool, develop a lesson, improve a model, test a claim, help another person establish their own installation, or build a world around knowledge that matters to them.

The future would acquire points of entry.

This is the psychological promise of practical hope: aspiration becoming connected to something a person can understand and do.

Assistance expands the person's possibilities

The ambition includes relief from burdens and the confidence to delegate.

People should be able to accept substantial help while retaining a meaningful relationship to its purpose and consequences. A capable assistant could make a task manageable, help a person learn, or free time for something more important to them.

Success would include a person becoming more capable of choosing how much to do directly, how much to learn, and how much to entrust to others.

Greater machine capability could become a felt expansion of human possibility.

11A more integrated experience of meaning

The breadth of the corpus makes another psychological hypothesis available: people might experience more of their commitments as belonging together.

Someone may care deeply about faith, intellectual honesty, mathematical precision, creative work, and the well-being of others. A successful undertaking that gives those commitments distinct and productive roles could help that person bring more of themselves into their work.

Martela and Steger distinguish three dimensions of meaning in life: coherence, purpose, and significance. Coherence concerns comprehensibility; purpose concerns direction; significance concerns life's value. Their work supplies a conceptual framework for understanding these differences.15

The programme could contribute to each dimension in its own way.

Coherence could grow through clearer relationships among understanding, conviction, and action. Purpose could grow through worthwhile tasks that connect personal effort to shared aims. Significance could be experienced through participation in a setting where a person's judgment, contribution, and development matter.

This possibility depends on the quality of the connections. Mathematical work earns mathematical confidence. Physical claims earn confidence through their relationship with evidence. Software earns confidence through what it reliably does. Ethical commitments earn credibility through how people are treated.

Keeping those standards visible allows integration to remain open to learning.

For people seeking to follow Jesus, the programme's success could make kenosis feel generative in contemporary life. A theological commitment would have helped produce useful inquiry, trustworthy tools, and practices that expand participation. Faith could be experienced as a source of serious construction and service.

Other people could encounter the same achievements through different convictions. They might value accountable systems, intellectual openness, creative freedom, or mutual support without adopting the programme's theology.

That freedom belongs inside the vision. People can contribute to a common undertaking and retain different accounts of its ultimate meaning.

The hoped-for psychological effect is a stronger relationship between what a person cares about and what they can actually do. Intellectual life, practical work, spiritual commitment, and concern for others could become more mutually intelligible.

12How local success could change collective expectations

An experience becomes culturally consequential when people can carry it into another setting.

Someone who has worked within an intelligible, participatory arrangement gains a concrete point of comparison. They may bring that experience into a workplace, school, research group, religious community, or public institution. They can describe what worked, explain why it mattered, and help reproduce it.

Bandura's account of collective efficacy concerns shared belief in a group's ability to produce effects through coordinated action. His synthesis connects that belief with collective commitment, resilience, and accomplishment.16

The programme's larger hypothesis is that successful participation could make effective cooperation feel more attainable.

A community could acquire confidence through completing useful work together. That confidence would have a practical basis: people would know some of the methods, possess some of the tools, and understand something about how to handle disagreement.

The effect could extend to expectations of leadership. Participants might increasingly expect a capable leader or system to explain its purposes, respect delegated authority, support correction, and develop other people's abilities.

A successful example gives those expectations something concrete to point to. It supplies methods and evidence alongside aspiration.

The wider consequence could be a change in the perceived relationship between care and competence. Serving others could become recognisable as an organising principle capable of producing sophisticated, dependable work.

That is a substantial cultural possibility. It would make humane ambition easier to discuss in practical terms, and give people more ways to act on it.

The spread would depend on access, intelligibility, adaptation, and sustained results. Different communities would need to make the work their own. The most valuable diffusion would include new applications and improvements that the original programme could not have anticipated.

13The kenotic test of success

ROOM TO QUESTION

Let correction matter

The passages on who can challenge, and whether correction can change a claim.

  • Who can challenge the funder or reviewer? ↗
  • When correction protects itself ↗

The programme's character would become especially clear when people question it.

A participant might challenge a scientific inference, reject a theological interpretation, change a design, or use part of the work for a purpose I did not foresee. Their ability to do so responsibly would be part of the capability the programme had helped create.

I want people to understand the work well enough to exercise that judgment.

There is a useful psychological connection here. Edmondson's field study of 51 teams in one manufacturing company found an association between psychological safety and learning behaviour. Psychological safety concerns a shared sense that interpersonal risk taking is safe within the team.17

The programme-specific hypothesis is that correction can become compatible with dignity and belonging. People can identify a mistake, admit uncertainty, ask a difficult question, or propose a revision and continue to participate.

Formal permission alone is insufficient. The social experience must make the permission usable. An objection route matters when someone can use it, be heard, and obtain a response.

Trust could become more precise in such an environment. Participants could learn what a system does well, where its limits lie, and how to revise their confidence when evidence changes. An intelligible record and effective correction could make substantial cooperation possible without asking people to abandon judgment.

This also applies to me.

A strong programme should enable people to extend useful work beyond my own choices. It should preserve the conditions for criticism and continuation. Its value should become increasingly available through participants who possess their own understanding.

People who decline an interpretation, leave an arrangement, or choose another tool can still have been treated well. Their freedom helps reveal whether the undertaking is living by its own account of power.

The kenotic test is concrete: what room does success make for other people?

14The path from programme to public possibility

The full arc has several distinct movements.

First, a commitment gives the work direction. Power should serve life. Intelligence should contribute to the good of persons. Inquiry should return understanding that others can use.

Second, disciplined inquiry gives that commitment substance. Arguments become clearer, mathematical constructions become exact, experiments become discriminating, and implementations become dependable.

Third, useful achievements become accessible experiences. People can learn the tools, inspect relevant reasons, contribute material, obtain help, and make consequential choices.

Fourth, participation produces capabilities people can retain. They acquire understanding, methods, skills, relationships, and work they can carry forward.

Fifth, those capabilities change what people regard as possible together. A successful arrangement becomes a point of comparison, a source of practical hope, and a resource for building elsewhere.

These movements reinforce one another. People using a tool discover requirements its designers missed. A failed experiment clarifies the theory. A participant's criticism improves the rules. An unfamiliar community gives an established method a new application.

The programme should be able to learn through those encounters.

There will be different public responses. Some people may experience renewed religious confidence. Some may be drawn to the scientific or technical work. Others may care most about ownership, education, creative freedom, or help with a practical task. Sceptical participation may be as valuable as enthusiastic participation when it improves the work.

Ethical communication should make the strongest positive case that the evidence can carry. It should tell people what has been achieved, what remains open, what participation involves, and what they can expect to retain.

I want the work to earn attention through usefulness and intelligibility, and to sustain that attention through trustworthy practice.

The larger cultural hypothesis is therefore about a possibility becoming available in many places: people encounter capable power that respects their agency, learn how it works, and bring that experience into the making of other institutions.

15What would count as evidence

A WORKING SCROLL

Open to correction

Read. Question. Examine the evidence. Follow the open work.

  • What would change this account ↗
  • A complete protocol is not a confirmed result ↗

A programme of this scope needs success to remain inspectable.

Different achievements call for different evidence:

Kind of claimEvidence that would support it
MathematicalPrecise definitions, valid arguments, explicit assumptions, reproducible calculations, and independent scrutiny
PhysicalA specified carrier and mechanism, discriminating observations, credible controls, and reproducible comparison with alternatives
ComputationalCorrect behaviour within stated conditions, enforced authority boundaries, traceable changes, and successful handling of relevant failures
Authoring and learningPeople understanding the relevant model, completing useful tasks, correcting mistakes, and adapting material
PsychologicalEvidence of meaningful choice, growing competence, well-calibrated trust, and changes in participants' experience
InstitutionalUsable participation, fair procedures, protection, sustainable operation, and opportunities for correction
CulturalPractices reproduced across settings, durable changes in expectations, and useful work continuing beyond the original programme

This is a research agenda, not a list of outcomes already established.

The psychological hypothesis can be made specific. After participating, are people better able to explain consequential operations? Can they pursue goals they chose? Can they detect mistakes and judge when to rely on an agent? Can they disagree, refuse, and propose alternatives? Can they create useful work with others and continue with less assistance when they want to?

The evidence should include observed performance, people's accounts of their experience, and appropriate established measures. Repeated observations can distinguish an initial burst of enthusiasm from lasting capability. Comparisons with other ways of working can help identify what the programme contributes.

Where causal claims are made, the evaluation design must address alternative explanations, including prior motivation, selection into the programme, facilitator skill, and novelty. Reports from people who struggle, decline, or leave are part of understanding the result.

The present psychology literature provides plausible mechanisms. It does not establish this programme's effects or guarantee a worldwide transformation. The task is to test whether the intended conditions become real experiences and whether those experiences produce durable benefits.

The same discipline applies across the undertaking. Technical success can give us a reliable tool. A mathematical result can give us a precise structure. A theological argument can articulate a reason for hope and action. Their connections should be evaluated through the work each connection actually enables.

That is how confidence can become more substantial as the programme develops.

16A commitment and an invitation

I intend to give this work the full force of my conviction, imagination, and practical effort.

I want to understand reality deeply enough to discover useful structure. I want to make systems intelligible enough for people to shape them. I want increasingly capable intelligence to serve human life. I want the things we build to leave people with more room to understand, choose, create, cooperate, and care.

Following Jesus is central to that purpose. I take his self-giving as a standard for what power should become in relation to others.

The work is an invitation to bring mathematics, experiments, criticism, craftsmanship, experience, faith, imagination, and the willingness to build. Different contributions can strengthen the undertaking while retaining their own voices.

Success would include people whose abilities and purposes carry the work beyond its starting point. They would make discoveries I did not make, build worlds I did not imagine, and correct things I had not understood.

The psychological hypothesis is that such success could change what the future feels like to the people who encounter it. Human flourishing could become more practically credible. Participation could feel more available. Hope could acquire routes, roles, and shared work.

There is something worth building, and people can have a real place in building it.

That is the full arc I want to pursue: from an account of power, through disciplined understanding and accountable construction, into capabilities that people can keep and a world they can help author.

Power must serve life. I intend to make that conviction something people can experience.

GGlossary

TermMeaning in this essay
KenosisChrist's self-emptying, used here as a theological basis for power exercised through service, protection, and room for others' agency
AgencyA person's meaningful ability to understand, choose, act, and influence matters that concern them
AdmissionThe decision that a proposed representation or operation satisfies the applicable conditions for use
EffectAn action that changes or interacts with something beyond a calculation, such as writing a file or changing a displayed interface
AuthorityThe legitimate permission and responsibility to act within a specified scope
Language-oriented programmingOrganising software through languages suited to the concepts and activities being expressed
Partial self-hostingExpressing substantial parts of a system's own construction or operation within its languages while retaining an external implementation base
Programme algebraThe corpus's structured representation of research objects, transformations, evidence, assumptions, and authority
Collective efficacyShared belief in a group's ability to accomplish effects through coordinated action

SSources and reading notes

The corpus sources below establish what the programme describes and claims. They are not independent certification of every proposed scientific result or future social effect. The psychology sources support particular mechanisms and distinctions; the wider hypothesis developed in this essay remains an application to be tested.

Repository links point to living source documents and may change as the work develops.

  1. Christian scriptural foundations. Philippians 2:3–11 and Mark 10:42–45, United States Conference of Catholic Bishops. The programme's applications to computing and institutions are constructive interpretations of these commitments.
  2. Aaron Alderman, “Kenotic Governance: Tri-Omni Theism and Shared Responsibility in a Lawful World.” Corpus source. A philosophical and theological synthesis covering power, restraint, protection, responsibility, and restoration.
  3. Aaron Alderman, “The Locally Invariant Carrier and Its Mirror Face.” Corpus source. Presents the symplectic and primitive-form construction and distinguishes its mathematics from open physical identification.
  4. Aaron Alderman, “The Admissibility Frontier.” Corpus source. Develops the programme's questions about composition, transformation, selection, measurement, and preservation of discriminating records.
  5. Martin Fowler, “Language Workbenches: The Killer-App for Domain Specific Languages?” 2005. Original essay. Primary exposition of the language-oriented programming tradition and language workbenches.
  6. Worldwright, “Architecture.” Project documentation. Defines the roles of Temple, Sourcery, and Worldwright; describes authored representations, source ownership, native mechanisms, and present boundaries.
  7. Aaron Alderman website, “One authoring path.” Authoring documentation. Describes the authored workflow, division of responsibility with the native host, validation, snapshot rechecking, and rollback.
  8. Aaron Alderman website, process-source compiler. Executable process source. Includes the explicit candidate scope and admitted: false result discussed in this essay.
  9. Jerome H. Saltzer and Michael D. Schroeder, “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” 1975. Author-hosted paper. Foundational treatment of protection mechanisms, principals, permissions, capabilities, and protection domains.
  10. Aaron Alderman, “Programme Algebra Parallel Lane.” Corpus source. Describes typed research representations and the retention of assumptions, losses, evidence, and authority through transformations.
  11. Aaron Alderman, “Optional endpoints: practical hope, speculative arcs, mythic readings and theology.” Corpus source. Distinguishes practical research returns from optional interpretations offered under explicit premises.
  12. Worldwright, “Worldwright's operating model.” Project documentation. Describes free access under applicable licences, paid setup and teaching, voluntary support, user independence, and responsibility for costs.
  13. Richard M. Ryan and Edward L. Deci, “Self-Determination Theory and the Facilitation of Intrinsic Motivation, Social Development, and Well-Being.” American Psychologist 55(1), 2000, 68–78. Original paper. A theoretical and empirical synthesis concerning autonomy, competence, and relatedness; not an evaluation of this programme.
  14. C. R. Snyder and colleagues, “The will and the ways: development and validation of an individual-differences measure of hope.” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 60(4), 1991, 570–585. Primary abstract and bibliographic record. Develops the agency-and-pathways model and a measure of hope; it does not establish the effects of this proposed intervention.
  15. Frank Martela and Michael F. Steger, “The three meanings of meaning in life: Distinguishing coherence, purpose, and significance.” The Journal of Positive Psychology 11(5), 2016, 531–545. Article DOI. A conceptual analysis of three dimensions of meaning.
  16. Albert Bandura, “Exercise of Human Agency Through Collective Efficacy.” Current Directions in Psychological Science 9(3), 2000. Primary publication page. A research synthesis concerning collective agency and shared beliefs about coordinated accomplishment.
  17. Amy Edmondson, “Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams.” Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2), 1999, 350–383. Article DOI. A field study of 51 teams in one manufacturing company; its observational findings support a bounded connection between psychological safety and learning behaviour.
